preamble: Deglottalization: the velar ejective [kʼ] loses its glottalic airstream and merges with plain [k]. In Akkadian, Geers's law turns ḳ (Proto-Semitic *kʼ) into k when the same root also contains ṣ, which outranks it in stability, regardless of position. Fallon (2002) documents full or partial mergers of ejectives with plain stops in Omotic (Yemsa word-initially), Jicaquean and Lezgian dialects. Modern Hebrew and Cypriot Maronite Arabic reach the same endpoint indirectly via uvular q (*kʼ > q > k).

examples.note: ḳ > k next to ṣ; Arabic qaṣara 'shorten, restrict' keeps both emphatics. A rare exception is ḳaṣû beside regular kaṣû 'cold' (Streck 2011).

languageExamples.language: Biblical Hebrew to Israeli Hebrew (via q)

examples.note: Eastern Jicaque (Tol) ʔas debuccalized instead (Campbell & Oltrogge 1980).
Bender (1988), cited in Fallon (2002); elsewhere *kʼ gives ʔ in Yemsa (zeʔu 'red' < *zokʼ), so the outcome depends on position.
